intuition: A tree's outer leaves are farthest from its center. Remove all current leaves together, then repeat with the smaller tree. When one or two vertices remain, they are the central choices of root that give the minimum height. Removing one leaf at a time would lose this symmetry.

Leaves have degree one. Removing all of them together shortens every outer branch by one edge and preserves the center of the longest paths. Their neighbors may become new leaves for the next round. Degree counts allow this update without physically deleting every adjacency-list entry.

Remove a complete layer before deciding whether to continue. A tree center may be a single vertex or the two vertices of a central edge, so stop when at most two vertices remain. The single-vertex input needs a separate return because its vertex has degree zero and would not enter a degree-one queue.
Layered removal does linear work: each vertex becomes a leaf once, and each edge triggers only a bounded number of degree updates.

In a star, removing its simultaneous outer leaves can first lower the center to degree one and enqueue it, then lower it to zero as the last leaf is removed. It still belongs to the answer: the queue holds vertices exposed by this complete layer, and remaining already says one vertex survives.
Degree zero here means no remaining edge, not that the center was removed.

steps: For n=6 with edges [[3,0],[3,1],[3,2],[3,4],[5,4]], initial leaves are 0,1,2,5.
There are six remaining vertices; removing this four-vertex layer will leave two.
Removing 0 and 1 lowers node 3’s degree from 4 to 2.
Removing 2 lowers node 3’s degree to 1, so enqueue 3 as a new leaf.
Removing 5 lowers node 4’s degree to 1, so enqueue 4.
Stop with two remaining vertices and return [3,4]; either is a minimum-height root.

codeNotes.note: Freeze the current outer layer so newly exposed leaves are not removed in the same round.
Track how many vertices survive, stopping at one or two centers.
A neighbor becomes part of the next outside layer exactly when only one live connection remains.

keyDecision: Remove a whole leaf layer before counting the next layer. Stop with at most two vertices.

concept.question: Why do the centers of a tree survive peeling its outer leaves?
intuition: Trying every root and measuring its farthest distance repeats long traversals. A tree’s longest paths are bounded by outer leaves, so choosing a root closer to their middle reduces the worst distance.

Remove all current leaves together, then repeat on the smaller tree. Peeling trims both ends of every longest path equally. The final one or two nodes are its centers and give the smallest possible rooted height.
concept.observation: Peel an entire leaf layer simultaneously; stop when at most two nodes remain.
approach: Remove a complete layer of degree-one leaves and update neighboring degrees.
Return the final one or two centers.
concept.correctness: A farthest vertex from a tree root is a leaf. Removing all leaves shortens the competing longest routes from both ends without changing which surviving vertices minimize maximum distance. Repeating this symmetric reduction leaves the middle vertex or middle pair of a diameter, the only possible minimum-height roots.

complexity.explanation: Each node enters a leaf layer once and each edge is removed once. Neighbor lists, degrees, and layer queues use linear time and storage.

pitfalls: Peel an entire leaf layer simultaneously; stop when at most two nodes remain.
The input must be a connected acyclic tree.

illustrations.caption: Peel all leaves together. Equal trimming from the ends leaves the one or two centers of the tree.

scenes.title: Identify the outer layer
scenes.narration: In the six-node fixture, edges join 3 to 0,1,2,4 and 4 to 5. Nodes 0,1,2,5 are leaves.
scenes.decision: Only a node with one remaining neighbor is in the current outer layer.

scenes.title: Peel both ends together
scenes.narration: Removing leaves 0,1,2,5 leaves just the edge joining 3 and 4.
scenes.decision: A newly exposed leaf belongs to the next layer, not the layer being removed.

scenes.title: Two centers remain
scenes.narration: Rooting at 3 or 4 gives height two; either root reaches the opposite outer end in two edges. Return [3,4].
scenes.decision: With two surviving nodes, neither has a smaller maximum distance than the other.
